evidence_chunks.chunk_id: 0045_Lu 等 - 2025 - All-climate carbonate electrolyte with 2-sulfobenzoic anhydride additive leads the way to high-perfo::sec7::child10
evidence_chunks.content: Under more extreme conditions, discharge tests at $-20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ (Fig. 4a) revealed that cells with SA-based electrolyte delivered discharge capacities of 758.6, 702.2 and $638.2\mathrm{mAh}$ at $0.2\mathrm{C}$ , $0.5\mathrm{C}$ , and $1\mathrm{C}$ ( $1\mathrm{C} = 900\mathrm{mA}$ ), respectively, outperforming those with the baseline electrolyte, which exhibited 706.3, 636.8 and $563.6\mathrm{mAh}$ . These results confirm that SA facilitates higher energy density and improved capacity retention at low temperatures, rendering it well-suited for emergency storage applications in cold environments. In addition, the rate capability of sodium-ion batteries at ambient temperature is critical for practical deployment. High-rate performance enables rapid charge/discharge cycles, a requirement for power-intensive applications such as electric vehicles and portable electronics [27a,28]. As shown in Fig. 4d, the SA containing system exhibited superior rate capacity, indicating enhanced commercial viability. Long-term cycling at 1C was also evaluated at room temperature (Figs. 4c and S7). During extended cycling, the baseline electrolyte showed faster polarization growth, whereas the SA-based system demonstrated superior capacity retention and enhanced coulombic efficiency. These characteristics contribute to reduced energy losses and extended battery lifespan, which are advantageous for grid-scale and commercial energy storage [29].

evidence_chunks.content: Pouch cells were subjected to aging and pre-formation process, both conducted under pressure by charging from open-circuit voltage (OCV) to 3.8 V at 45 °C. Long-term cycling was carried out on a five-channel battery testing system. Cells were charged at a constant current of 900 mA to a cutoff voltage of 3.8 V, followed by a constant voltage hold at 3.8 V until the current decreased to 30 mA, and subsequently discharged at 900 mA down to 1.5 V. Discharge was carried out at 900 mA down to 1.5 V. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was measured using an AMETEK Solartron Analytical system over a frequency range of 100 kHz to 0.04 Hz. Galvanostatic intermittent titration technique (GITT) measurements were conducted using a discharge current of 45 mA, with a discharge duration of 1 h followed by a rest period of 2 h. Tafel analysis was conducted using Na|Na symmetric coin cells on an electrochemical workstation over a voltage range of -0.13 to 0.13 V. The intersection of the linear portions of the two semi-logarithmic curves indicates the exchange current, from which the exchange current density was determined by normalizing the current to the surface area of the coin cell. Linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) was conducted on a CHI660E electrochemical workstation (Chenhua, Shanghai).

## 配方筛选结果
获得文献支持的候选：SA-1wt-Lu2025。

### 候选资料：SA-1wt-Lu2025（通过筛选）
以下为候选记录中的组成，配制时须核对所引原文的比例基准与用量。
盐：NaPF6；浓度：1 mol L⁻¹；NaPF6：1 mol L⁻¹；溶剂：EC, EMC；溶剂比例（质量）：EC=0.3, EMC=0.7；添加剂：2-sulfobenzoic anhydride (SA)；添加剂用量：2-sulfobenzoic anhydride (SA)=1 wt%。

A baseline electrolyte was prepared by dissolving NaPF $_6$ (1 mol/L) into a mixed solvent of EC and EMC (weight ratio 3:7). To formulate a functional electrolyte, 1 wt% 2-Sulfobenzoic anhydride (SA) was added to the baseline system. The NFM cathode and hard carbon (HC) anode active materials were procured from Jiangsu Xiangying New Energy Technology Co., Ltd. and Kuraray Co., Ltd., respectively. The NFM cathode slurry consisted of 94.5 wt% NFM, 1.8 wt% PVDF, 1 wt% carbon nanotubes (CNT), 2.5 wt% Super P, and 0.2 wt% maleic acid dispersed in $N$ -methylpyrrolidone (NMP), and was cast onto aluminum foil. The HC anode was composed of 95 wt% HC,

![](images/8bfcb630e9de984c98fbfc69f2dd0cb440e9bd8293373fa0ec9806e9fb6d55de.jpg)  
Fig. 1. 2-Sulfobenzoic anhydride (SA) is introduced as electrolyte additive to enhance the electrochemical performance of pouch SIBs.

1.5 wt% carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC), 2 wt% styrene-butadiene rubber (SBR), and 1.5 wt% Super P. A Celgard 2700 membrane (Xingyuan Materials Co., Ltd.) was employed as the separator. The areal mass loadings of the cathode and anode were 33.0 and 20.1 mg/cm $^{2}$ , respectively, with a negative-to-positive (N/P) capacity ratio of 1.1 (based on theoretical capacity calculation).

Sodium hexafluorophosphate (NaPF $_6$ ), ethylene carbonate (EC), and methyl ethyl carbonate (EMC) were supplied by Guangzhou Tinci Materials Technology Co., Ltd. A baseline electrolyte was prepared by dissolving NaPF $_6$ (1 mol/L) into a mixed solvent of EC and EMC (weight ratio 3:7). To formulate a functional electrolyte, 1 wt% 2-Sulfobenzoic anhydride (SA) was added to the baseline system. The NFM cathode and hard carbon (HC) anode active materials were procured from Jiangsu Xiangying New Energy Technology Co., Ltd. and Kuraray Co., Ltd., respectively. The NFM cathode slurry consisted of 94.5 wt% NFM, 1.8 wt% PVDF, 1 wt% carbon nanotubes (CNT), 2.5 wt% Super P, and 0.2 wt% maleic acid dispersed in $N$ -methylpyrrolidone (NMP), and was cast onto aluminum foil. The HC anode was composed of 95 wt% HC,

![](images/8bfcb630e9de984c98fbfc69f2dd0cb440e9bd8293373fa0ec9806e9fb6d55de.jpg)

1.5 wt% carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC), 2 wt% styrene-butadiene rubber (SBR), and 1.5 wt% Super P. A Celgard 2700 membrane (Xingyuan Materials Co., Ltd.) was employed as the separator. source_refs.raw_quote: Under more extreme conditions, discharge tests at $-20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ (Fig. 4a) revealed that cells with SA-based electrolyte delivered discharge capacities of 758.6, 702.2 and $638.2\mathrm{mAh}$ at $0.2\mathrm{C}$ , $0.5\mathrm{C}$ , and $1\mathrm{C}$ ( $1\mathrm{C} = 900\mathrm{mA}$ ), respectively, outperforming those with the baseline electrolyte, which exhibited 706.3, 636.8 and $563.6\mathrm{mAh}$ . These results confirm that SA facilitates higher energy density and improved capacity retention at low temperatures, rendering it well-suited for emergency storage applications in cold environments. In addition, the rate capability of sodium-ion batteries at ambient temperature is critical for practical deployment. High-rate performance enables rapid charge/discharge cycles, a requirement for power-intensive applications such as electric vehicles and portable electronics [27a,28]. As shown in Fig. 4d, the SA containing system exhibited superior rate capacity, indicating enhanced commercial viability. Long-term cycling at 1C was also evaluated at room temperature (Figs. 4c and S7). During extended cycling, the baseline electrolyte showed faster polarization growth, whereas the SA-based system demonstrated superior capacity retention and enhanced coulombic efficiency. These characteristics contribute to reduced energy losses and extended battery lifespan, which are advantageous for grid-scale and commercial energy storage [29].

Long-term cycling was carried out on a five-channel battery testing system. Cells were charged at a constant current of 900 mA to a cutoff voltage of 3.8 V, followed by a constant voltage hold at 3.8 V until the current decreased to 30 mA, and subsequently discharged at 900 mA down to 1.5 V. Discharge was carried out at 900 mA down to 1.5 V. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was measured using an AMETEK Solartron Analytical system over a frequency range of 100 kHz to 0.04 Hz. Galvanostatic intermittent titration technique (GITT) measurements were conducted using a discharge current of 45 mA, with a discharge duration of 1 h followed by a rest period of 2 h. Tafel analysis was conducted using Na|Na symmetric coin cells on an electrochemical workstation over a voltage range of -0.13 to 0.13 V. The intersection of the linear portions of the two semi-logarithmic curves indicates the exchange current, from which the exchange current density was determined by normalizing the current to the surface area of the coin cell. Linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) was conducted on a CHI660E electrochemical workstation (Chenhua, Shanghai).

On the contrary, the large amount of the additive forms a too thick SEI film, increasing the impedance. The discharge rate performance of the battery with G1 is the worst, owing to the decomposition of the electrolyte to form the SEI film with a high impedance [24]. From the discharge voltage curves at 2.0 C in Fig. 1C, the battery with G1 showed the lowest discharge voltage plateau, indicating a large impedance at large discharge rates, which is consistent with the rate results. The discharge capacities at high and low temperatures are shown in Fig. 3A. When setting the discharge capacity of each battery at 25 °C and 0.5C as the initial capacity (100%), the discharge capacities of the batteries with G1, G2, G3 and G4 at -20 °C and 0.2 C were 67.35%, 75.07%, 76.45%, and 74.26%, respectively. Hence, the capacity of the battery with G3 (3% ADN) was most significantly increased by up to 13% (Fig. 3B). At -10 °C and 0.5 C, the capacities were 72%, 78.17%, 80.21%, and 77.84%, respectively, from which the battery with G3 still exhibited the best performance with a discharge capacity improvement of nearly 8% (Fig. 3C). Similar results were presented at 45 °C and 1.0 C, where the capacities were 70.88%, 79.76%, 81.38%, 75.99%, respectively, and the batteries of G3 increased the discharge capacity by 10.5% (Fig. 3D). Materials
The sodium hexafluorophosphate (NaPF $_6$ , 99.8% min), diethylene glycol dimethyl ether (G2, 99.8% min) and 2-methyloxolane (MO, 99.8% min) were purchased from DoDo Chem. Common ether electrolyte (CCE) was prepared by dissolving 0.8 M NaPF $_6$ in G2 solvent. Weakly solvated electrolyte (WSE) was prepared by dissolving 0.8 M NaPF $_6$ in MO solvent. Co-intercalated electrolyte (CIE) was prepared by dissolving 0.8 M NaPF $_6$ in G2: MO = 7:3 vol%. All electrolyte preparation processes were carried out in a glovebox filled with Ar (H $_2$ O < 0.1 ppm and O $_2$ < 0.1 ppm). The electrolyte salts and solvents we purchased are of anhydrous grade. After purchase, they are placed in the glove box for direct use.

Hard carbon (HC) materials were purchased from Baisige New Energy Co., Ltd. The HC negative electrode was prepared by mixing the active material, CMC (CMC2200, purchased from Daicel Corporation), SBR (BM-451B, purchased from Zeon Corporation) and conductive carbon black (weight ratio 92:1.5:3.5:3) in deionized water to form a homogeneous slurry. The slurry was spread on a copper foil (thickness 18 $\mu$ m) and dried at 80 °C for 8–12 h. Then, it was perforated into a circular electrode sheet with a diameter of 12 mm and a loading of 2.5–3.0 mg cm $^{-2}$ . Glass fiber (GF/D, Whatman) was used as separator and metallic sodium (purchased from Canrd Technology Co. Ltd.) was used as counter electrode. These components were assembled with HC negative electrode to assemble Na ||HC coin cells. The diameter of the glass fiber is 16 mm and the thickness is 0.68 mm. The diameter of the sodium metal electrode is 15.6 mm and the thickness is 0.4 mm.

The Ah-level pouch batteries were composed of O3-NaNi $_{1/3}$ Fe $_{1/3}$ Mn $_{1/3}$ O $_{2}$ (NFM) positive electrode and HC negative electrode coated on Al foil. The specific details and parameters are shown in Table S7.

source_refs.raw_quote: To verify the practical applicability of CIE, we assembled a 1.2 Ah (163 Wh kg $^{-1}$ ) pouch cell with O3-type NFM positive electrode and HC negative electrode (Fig. 6a). Figure 6b shows the cycling performance of the pouch cell at different temperatures. At 25 °C, the pouch cell provides a capacity of 1.18 Ah. As the temperature decreases, we verify the possibility of its operation at low temperatures, at -50 °C, the pouch cell still provides a capacity of 0.79 Ah (107 Wh kg $^{-1}$ ), demonstrating a significantly better low-temperature adaptability than that of conventional electrolytes. Moreover, even at -50 °C, the charge/discharge curve maintains a stable voltage plateau (Fig. 6c). Figure 6d shows the cycling performance of the pouch cell at -20 °C with 94.1% capacity retention after 300 cycles. In addition, in order to visually verify the practical application potential, the LED lights are continuously powered at a low temperature of -50 °C. The fully-charged state pouch cells keep the LED lights working for more than 10 hours (Fig. 6e). This demonstration confirms that the CIE has good prospects for practical applications, especially at low temperatures. We further compare our results with some previously reported low-temperature sodium-ion pouch cells (Fig. 6f, Table S6) $^{26,52-58}$ , and our work is comparable to most of the advanced reported works, which fully proves that the CIE developed by us has important application value for SIBs in cold environments.

source_refs.raw_quote: A multifunctional additive, 2-sulfobenzoic anhydride (SA), was synthesized from the readily available saccharin, then 1 % SA was added into carbonate-based electrolytes to enhance the performance of pouch sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) employing $NaNi_{0.33}Fe_{0.33}Mn_{0.33}O_{2}$ (NFM) cathodes and hard carbon (HC) anodes across a wide temperature range from $-20\ ^{\circ}C$ to $60\ ^{\circ}C$ . The commercial pouch cells delivered a capacity retention of 90.52 % after 300 cycles at room temperature and 92.28 % after 300 cycles at $45\ ^{\circ}C$ . Low-temperature rate performance at $-20\ ^{\circ}C$ and cycling at $-10\ ^{\circ}C$ further demonstrated the excellent adaptability of SA-containing electrolytes under sub-zero temperature. Moreover, under high-voltage operation at 4.0 V, the SA-containing electrolyte effectively suppressed capacity fading, resulting in an 11.44 % improvement in capacity retention. Compared to conventional commercial electrolytes, this electrolyte enables interfacial optimization by suppressing excessive growth of cathode and anode interphases, also it eliminates detrimental electrolyte components, tune the solvation structure and promote interfacial reaction kinetics. In situ gas analysis conducted during cycling at $45\ ^{\circ}C$ revealed that SA significantly inhibits gas-evolving side reactions, thereby ensuring the safety of SIBs.

Abstract: A commercially feasible sodium-ion pouch cell with a capacity of 650 mAh is fabricated using the ternary layered $\mathrm{Na_{0.76}Ni_{0.3}Fe_{0.4}Mn_{0.3}O_2}$ and the hard carbon as the cathode and anode materials, respectively. $1.0\mathrm{MNaPF}_6$ in the mixed carbonate solvents is served as the electrolyte. According to the calculation of the frontier molecular orbital energy, adiponitrile (ADN) has a stronger ability of electron donating than the carbonate solvents and thus is easier to be reduced on the surface of the cathode material to form the solid-electrolyte interphase (SEI) film, so ADN is selected as the electrolyte additive to improve the performance of sodium-ion battery for the first time.

2.2 Battery Assembly
$Na_{0.76}Ni_{0.3}Fe_{0.4}Mn_{0.3}O_{2}$ , carbon nanotubes (CNTs), polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF), and carbon black with the mass ratio of 92.5: 2.0: 3.5: 2.0 were mixed in pyrrolidone to form a uniform slurry, and then coated on a 14 um thick aluminum foil to prepare the cathode electrode. The areal density was measured to be 10.0 mg cm $^{-2}$ , and the compacted density was 2.1 g cm $^{-3}$ . To prepare the anode electrode, hard carbon (Kuraray), carbon black, cellulose sodium (CMC), and styrene butadiene rubber (SBR) with the mass ratio of 94.5: 1.0: 2.0: 2.5 were added in deionized water and stirred into a uniform slurry, and then coated on a 9 um thick copper foil with the areal and compacted densities of 4.31 mg cm $^{-2}$ and 1.4 g cm $^{-3}$ , respectively. The cathode, anode, and separator (20 μm polypropylene) were assembled into pouch cells with a designed capacity of 650 mAh, and the thickness, width, and length were 10, 68, and 127 mm, respectively. The cells were dried in vacuum (-99 kPa/80 °C) until the water content was less than 150 ppm. At a dewpoint of -40 °C, the electrolytes defined as G1, G2, G3, and G4 (Table 1) were injected into the cells. After packaging in vacuum at room temperature for 48 hours; the pouch cells were placed at the environment with 0.8 MPa and 45 °C and charged at 0.05 C for 180 min, followed by another charge at a constant current of 0.1 C for 360 min. Then, the pouch cells were punctuated in vacuum to remove excess electrolyte and gas generated by the side reactions during the charge process. Eventually, the cells were packaged again and cut the air-bags to obtain the finished batteries for testing.

source_refs.raw_quote: In summary, a commercially feasible sodium-ion pouch cell with $Na_{0.76}Ni_{0.3}Fe_{0.4}Mn_{0.3}O_{2}$ /hard carbon is fabricated in this work. According to the calculation of the frontier molecular orbital energy, the electrolyte additive adiponitrile (ADN) is selected as the electrolyte additive to improve the performance of sodium-ion battery for the first time, and the effects of the ADN on the performance improvement of the cathode material $Na_{0.76}Ni_{0.3}Fe_{0.4}Mn_{0.3}O_{2}$ are investigated for the first time. The results show that ADN can promote the formation of highly conductive and stable SEI film on the cathode material surface, and effectively improve the high-low-temperature performance and cycling stability of $Na_{0.76}Ni_{0.3}Fe_{0.4}Mn_{0.3}O_{2}$ as the cathode electrode material of sodium-ion batteries. In particular, the battery with 3% ADN shows the most obvious improvement, its discharge capacity increases by 10.5%, 8%, and 13% at the operating temperature of 45, -10, and -20 °C, respectively. For the cycling stability, the capacity retention rate of the battery without adding ADN drops rapidly to 75% after 40 cycles, while the capacity retention rate of the battery with 3% ADN can still reach 78% after 220 cycles. Adding ADN as electrolyte additive effectively improves the electrochemical performance of sodium ion batteries.

source_refs.raw_quote: To solve this problem, a CIE was designed in this work. The design principle is based on the following findings: there are always some solvents in the electrolyte that do not participate in the coordination and only act as ion transport media, which are called free solvents. For this reason, we replaced this part of free solvent with 2-methyloxolane (MO) which has a lower melting point ( $-136^{\circ}C$ , Table S1) and is less polar. Through this strategy, not only the co-embeddable solvation structure is retained and the ion transport kinetics are accelerated, but also the working temperature range of electrolyte in low-temperature environment is significantly widened by increasing the solvation entropy. To highlight the progressiveness of our designed electrolyte, we also used common co-intercalation ether electrolyte (CCE) and WSE as controls, and the specific electrolyte formulation is shown in Table S2. According to the optical photographs in Figure S1, CCE starts to have salt precipitation at $-30^{\circ}C$ , and it is even completely solidified at $-50^{\circ}C$ . On the other hand, WSE and our CIE remain liquid at $-50^{\circ}C$ , which effectively guarantees the possibility of electrolyte application at low temperatures. The ion transport mechanisms of various electrolytes at low temperatures are shown in Fig. 1, among which the CIE has the fastest ion transport rate due to the presence of the co-intercalation behavior.

source_refs.raw_quote: When the temperature is lower than -20 °C, the ionic conductivity of CCE decreases rapidly, which can be attributed to the precipitation of $NaPF_{6}$ in the electrolyte. While CIE maintains a high ionic conductivity at low temperatures and is always higher than that of WSE. Therefore, compared to the WSE, the CIE designed here can effectively solve the decrease in ionic conductivity and promote ion transport at low temperatures. In addition, we also tested the physical parameters of different electrolytes, such as the electrochemical window and transference number (Figs. S5, S6). Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were carried out to further investigate the solvation structure of the electrolyte under different temperature gradients. The radial distribution functions (RDF) of different electrolytes are shown in Fig. 2e,f and S7-8. In CCE, the average coordination number of G2 is 1.60 and that of PF $_{6}^{-}$ is 0.87. While in CIE, the coordination number of G2 decreases to 1.41, the coordination number of PF $_{6}^{-}$ increases to 1.10, and that of MO is 0.11. This is attributed to the introduction of MO which has a dipole interaction with G2, slightly weakening the coordination of G2 and Na $^{+}$ . In addition, MO hardly coordinates with Na $^{+}$ , which is consistent with the results of Raman and FTIR. In WSE, the average coordination number of MO is 0.93 and PF $_{6}^{-}$ is 3.05, constituting a typical aggregate-type (AGG) solvation structure rich in anions.

source_refs.chunk_id: 0033_Li 等 - 2026 - Enhanced sodium storage in hard carbon via solvent co-intercalation electrolyte enabling Ah-level po::sec6::child2
source_refs.paper_id: 0033_Li 等 - 2026 - Enhanced sodium storage in hard carbon via solvent co-intercalation electrolyte enabling Ah-level po
source_refs.raw_quote: The MO solvent is added into linear ether G2 to precisely regulate the solvation structure and expand the electrolyte's low-temperature range via an entropy-driven effect. Experiments and simulations reveal that the $Na^{+}-G2$ chelating coordination structure can be well co-embedded in HC negative electrode, avoiding the sluggish traditional desolvation process and significantly improving ion diffusion at low temperatures. Meanwhile, the high sodium salt dissociation ability of G2 ensures good ionic conductivity in electrolyte. And the dipole interaction between solvents drives an appropriate number of anions into the solvation sheath, inducing the formation of a thin layer of inorganic-rich SEI. This multi-scale synergistic design enables highly reversible and high-rate sodium storage at low temperatures. Consequently, the CIE enables HC to deliver an initial Coulombic efficiency of 80.5% at $-50\ ^{\circ}C$ and a capacity retention of 93% after 200 cycles. Moreover, an Ah-level full cell retains 163 Wh kg $^{-1}$ at 25 ${}^{\circ}C$ and 107 Wh kg $^{-1}$ at $-50\ ^{\circ}C$ . This study demonstrates the significance of the solvent co-embedding mechanism in improving low-temperature ion storage and provides a strategy for designing electrolytes toward cold environments.

citations.quote: A multifunctional additive, 2-sulfobenzoic anhydride (SA), was synthesized from the readily available saccharin, then 1 % SA was added into carbonate-based electrolytes to enhance the performance of pouch sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) employing $NaNi_{0.33}Fe_{0.33}Mn_{0.33}O_{2}$ (NFM) cathodes and hard carbon (HC) anodes across a wide temperature range from $-20\ ^{\circ}C$ to $60\ ^{\circ}C$ . The commercial pouch cells delivered a capacity retention of 90.52 % after 300 cycles at room temperature and 92.28 % after 300 cycles at $45\ ^{\circ}C$ . Low-temperature rate performance at $-20\ ^{\circ}C$ and cycling at $-10\ ^{\circ}C$ further demonstrated the excellent adaptability of SA-containing electrolytes under sub-zero temperature. Moreover, under high-voltage operation at 4.0 V, the SA-containing electrolyte effectively suppressed capacity fading, resulting in an 11.44 % improvement in capacity retention. Compared to conventional commercial electrolytes, this electrolyte enables interfacial optimization by suppressing excessive growth of cathode and anode interphases, also it eliminates detrimental electrolyte components, tune the solvation structure and promote interfacial reaction kinetics. In situ gas analysis conducted during cycling at $45\ ^{\circ}C$ revealed that SA significantly inhibits gas-evolving side reactions, thereby ensuring the safety of SIBs.

association_citations.quote: Pouch cells were subjected to aging and pre-formation process, both conducted under pressure by charging from open-circuit voltage (OCV) to 3.8 V at 45 °C. Long-term cycling was carried out on a five-channel battery testing system. Cells were charged at a constant current of 900 mA to a cutoff voltage of 3.8 V, followed by a constant voltage hold at 3.8 V until the current decreased to 30 mA, and subsequently discharged at 900 mA down to 1.5 V. Discharge was carried out at 900 mA down to 1.5 V. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was measured using an AMETEK Solartron Analytical system over a frequency range of 100 kHz to 0.04 Hz. Galvanostatic intermittent titration technique (GITT) measurements were conducted using a discharge current of 45 mA, with a discharge duration of 1 h followed by a rest period of 2 h. Tafel analysis was conducted using Na|Na symmetric coin cells on an electrochemical workstation over a voltage range of -0.13 to 0.13 V. The intersection of the linear portions of the two semi-logarithmic curves indicates the exchange current, from which the exchange current density was determined by normalizing the current to the surface area of the coin cell. Linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) was conducted on a CHI660E electrochemical workstation (Chenhua, Shanghai).

association_citations.quote: Under more extreme conditions, discharge tests at $-20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ (Fig. 4a) revealed that cells with SA-based electrolyte delivered discharge capacities of 758.6, 702.2 and $638.2\mathrm{mAh}$ at $0.2\mathrm{C}$ , $0.5\mathrm{C}$ , and $1\mathrm{C}$ ( $1\mathrm{C} = 900\mathrm{mA}$ ), respectively, outperforming those with the baseline electrolyte, which exhibited 706.3, 636.8 and $563.6\mathrm{mAh}$ . These results confirm that SA facilitates higher energy density and improved capacity retention at low temperatures, rendering it well-suited for emergency storage applications in cold environments. In addition, the rate capability of sodium-ion batteries at ambient temperature is critical for practical deployment. High-rate performance enables rapid charge/discharge cycles, a requirement for power-intensive applications such as electric vehicles and portable electronics [27a,28]. As shown in Fig. 4d, the SA containing system exhibited superior rate capacity, indicating enhanced commercial viability. Long-term cycling at 1C was also evaluated at room temperature (Figs. 4c and S7). During extended cycling, the baseline electrolyte showed faster polarization growth, whereas the SA-based system demonstrated superior capacity retention and enhanced coulombic efficiency. These characteristics contribute to reduced energy losses and extended battery lifespan, which are advantageous for grid-scale and commercial energy storage [29].

Abstract: A commercially feasible sodium-ion pouch cell with a capacity of 650 mAh is fabricated using the ternary layered $\mathrm{Na_{0.76}Ni_{0.3}Fe_{0.4}Mn_{0.3}O_2}$ and the hard carbon as the cathode and anode materials, respectively. $1.0\mathrm{MNaPF}_6$ in the mixed carbonate solvents is served as the electrolyte. According to the calculation of the frontier molecular orbital energy, adiponitrile (ADN) has a stronger ability of electron donating than the carbonate solvents and thus is easier to be reduced on the surface of the cathode material to form the solid-electrolyte interphase (SEI) film, so ADN is selected as the electrolyte additive to improve the performance of sodium-ion battery for the first time.

citations.quote:
2.2 Battery Assembly
$Na_{0.76}Ni_{0.3}Fe_{0.4}Mn_{0.3}O_{2}$ , carbon nanotubes (CNTs), polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF), and carbon black with the mass ratio of 92.5: 2.0: 3.5: 2.0 were mixed in pyrrolidone to form a uniform slurry, and then coated on a 14 um thick aluminum foil to prepare the cathode electrode. The areal density was measured to be 10.0 mg cm $^{-2}$ , and the compacted density was 2.1 g cm $^{-3}$ . To prepare the anode electrode, hard carbon (Kuraray), carbon black, cellulose sodium (CMC), and styrene butadiene rubber (SBR) with the mass ratio of 94.5: 1.0: 2.0: 2.5 were added in deionized water and stirred into a uniform slurry, and then coated on a 9 um thick copper foil with the areal and compacted densities of 4.31 mg cm $^{-2}$ and 1.4 g cm $^{-3}$ , respectively. The cathode, anode, and separator (20 μm polypropylene) were assembled into pouch cells with a designed capacity of 650 mAh, and the thickness, width, and length were 10, 68, and 127 mm, respectively. The cells were dried in vacuum (-99 kPa/80 °C) until the water content was less than 150 ppm. At a dewpoint of -40 °C, the electrolytes defined as G1, G2, G3, and G4 (Table 1) were injected into the cells. After packaging in vacuum at room temperature for 48 hours; the pouch cells were placed at the environment with 0.8 MPa and 45 °C and charged at 0.05 C for 180 min, followed by another charge at a constant current of 0.1 C for 360 min. Then, the pouch cells were punctuated in vacuum to remove excess electrolyte and gas generated by the side reactions during the charge process. Eventually, the cells were packaged again and cut the air-bags to obtain the finished batteries for testing.

citations.chunk_id: 0061_Song 等 - 2018 - The effects of the functional electrolyte additive on the cathode material Na076Ni03Fe04Mn03O2 f::sec8::child0
citations.quote: In summary, a commercially feasible sodium-ion pouch cell with $Na_{0.76}Ni_{0.3}Fe_{0.4}Mn_{0.3}O_{2}$ /hard carbon is fabricated in this work. According to the calculation of the frontier molecular orbital energy, the electrolyte additive adiponitrile (ADN) is selected as the electrolyte additive to improve the performance of sodium-ion battery for the first time, and the effects of the ADN on the performance improvement of the cathode material $Na_{0.76}Ni_{0.3}Fe_{0.4}Mn_{0.3}O_{2}$ are investigated for the first time. The results show that ADN can promote the formation of highly conductive and stable SEI film on the cathode material surface, and effectively improve the high-low-temperature performance and cycling stability of $Na_{0.76}Ni_{0.3}Fe_{0.4}Mn_{0.3}O_{2}$ as the cathode electrode material of sodium-ion batteries. In particular, the battery with 3% ADN shows the most obvious improvement, its discharge capacity increases by 10.5%, 8%, and 13% at the operating temperature of 45, -10, and -20 °C, respectively. For the cycling stability, the capacity retention rate of the battery without adding ADN drops rapidly to 75% after 40 cycles, while the capacity retention rate of the battery with 3% ADN can still reach 78% after 220 cycles. Adding ADN as electrolyte additive effectively improves the electrochemical performance of sodium ion batteries.

citations.quote: When the little amount of the additive is used, the formed SEI film is not dense enough. On the contrary, the large amount of the additive forms a too thick SEI film, increasing the impedance. The discharge rate performance of the battery with G1 is the worst, owing to the decomposition of the electrolyte to form the SEI film with a high impedance [24]. From the discharge voltage curves at 2.0 C in Fig. 1C, the battery with G1 showed the lowest discharge voltage plateau, indicating a large impedance at large discharge rates, which is consistent with the rate results. The discharge capacities at high and low temperatures are shown in Fig. 3A. When setting the discharge capacity of each battery at 25 °C and 0.5C as the initial capacity (100%), the discharge capacities of the batteries with G1, G2, G3 and G4 at -20 °C and 0.2 C were 67.35%, 75.07%, 76.45%, and 74.26%, respectively. Hence, the capacity of the battery with G3 (3% ADN) was most significantly increased by up to 13% (Fig. 3B). At -10 °C and 0.5 C, the capacities were 72%, 78.17%, 80.21%, and 77.84%, respectively, from which the battery with G3 still exhibited the best performance with a discharge capacity improvement of nearly 8% (Fig. 3C). Similar results were presented at 45 °C and 1.0 C, where the capacities were 70.88%, 79.76%, 81.38%, 75.99%, respectively, and the batteries of G3 increased the discharge capacity by 10.5% (Fig. 3D). The specific discharge capacities at different temperatures are shown in Fig. 4.

citations.quote: $Na_{0.76}Ni_{0.3}Fe_{0.4}Mn_{0.3}O_{2}$ , carbon nanotubes (CNTs), polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF), and carbon black with the mass ratio of 92.5: 2.0: 3.5: 2.0 were mixed in pyrrolidone to form a uniform slurry, and then coated on a 14 um thick aluminum foil to prepare the cathode electrode. The areal density was measured to be 10.0 mg cm $^{-2}$ , and the compacted density was 2.1 g cm $^{-3}$ . To prepare the anode electrode, hard carbon (Kuraray), carbon black, cellulose sodium (CMC), and styrene butadiene rubber (SBR) with the mass ratio of 94.5: 1.0: 2.0: 2.5 were added in deionized water and stirred into a uniform slurry, and then coated on a 9 um thick copper foil with the areal and compacted densities of 4.31 mg cm $^{-2}$ and 1.4 g cm $^{-3}$ , respectively. The cathode, anode, and separator (20 μm polypropylene) were assembled into pouch cells with a designed capacity of 650 mAh, and the thickness, width, and length were 10, 68, and 127 mm, respectively. The cells were dried in vacuum (-99 kPa/80 °C) until the water content was less than 150 ppm. At a dewpoint of -40 °C, the electrolytes defined as G1, G2, G3, and G4 (Table 1) were injected into the cells. After packaging in vacuum at room temperature for 48 hours; the pouch cells were placed at the environment with 0.8 MPa and 45 °C and charged at 0.05 C for 180 min, followed by another charge at a constant current of 0.1 C for 360 min.

Materials
The sodium hexafluorophosphate (NaPF $_6$ , 99.8% min), diethylene glycol dimethyl ether (G2, 99.8% min) and 2-methyloxolane (MO, 99.8% min) were purchased from DoDo Chem. Common ether electrolyte (CCE) was prepared by dissolving 0.8 M NaPF $_6$ in G2 solvent. Weakly solvated electrolyte (WSE) was prepared by dissolving 0.8 M NaPF $_6$ in MO solvent. Co-intercalated electrolyte (CIE) was prepared by dissolving 0.8 M NaPF $_6$ in G2: MO = 7:3 vol%. All electrolyte preparation processes were carried out in a glovebox filled with Ar (H $_2$ O < 0.1 ppm and O $_2$ < 0.1 ppm). The electrolyte salts and solvents we purchased are of anhydrous grade. After purchase, they are placed in the glove box for direct use.

Hard carbon (HC) materials were purchased from Baisige New Energy Co., Ltd. The HC negative electrode was prepared by mixing the active material, CMC (CMC2200, purchased from Daicel Corporation), SBR (BM-451B, purchased from Zeon Corporation) and conductive carbon black (weight ratio 92:1.5:3.5:3) in deionized water to form a homogeneous slurry. The slurry was spread on a copper foil (thickness 18 $\mu$ m) and dried at 80 °C for 8–12 h. Then, it was perforated into a circular electrode sheet with a diameter of 12 mm and a loading of 2.5–3.0 mg cm $^{-2}$ . Glass fiber (GF/D, Whatman) was used as separator and metallic sodium (purchased from Canrd Technology Co. Ltd.) was used as counter electrode. These components were assembled with HC negative electrode to assemble Na ||HC coin cells. The diameter of the glass fiber is 16 mm and the thickness is 0.68 mm. The diameter of the sodium metal electrode is 15.6 mm and the thickness is 0.4 mm.

The Ah-level pouch batteries were composed of O3-NaNi $_{1/3}$ Fe $_{1/3}$ Mn $_{1/3}$ O $_{2}$ (NFM) positive electrode and HC negative electrode coated on Al foil. The specific details and parameters are shown in Table S7.

citations.quote: To verify the practical applicability of CIE, we assembled a 1.2 Ah (163 Wh kg $^{-1}$ ) pouch cell with O3-type NFM positive electrode and HC negative electrode (Fig. 6a). Figure 6b shows the cycling performance of the pouch cell at different temperatures. At 25 °C, the pouch cell provides a capacity of 1.18 Ah. As the temperature decreases, we verify the possibility of its operation at low temperatures, at -50 °C, the pouch cell still provides a capacity of 0.79 Ah (107 Wh kg $^{-1}$ ), demonstrating a significantly better low-temperature adaptability than that of conventional electrolytes. Moreover, even at -50 °C, the charge/discharge curve maintains a stable voltage plateau (Fig. 6c). Figure 6d shows the cycling performance of the pouch cell at -20 °C with 94.1% capacity retention after 300 cycles. In addition, in order to visually verify the practical application potential, the LED lights are continuously powered at a low temperature of -50 °C. The fully-charged state pouch cells keep the LED lights working for more than 10 hours (Fig. 6e). citations.quote: To solve this problem, a CIE was designed in this work. The design principle is based on the following findings: there are always some solvents in the electrolyte that do not participate in the coordination and only act as ion transport media, which are called free solvents. For this reason, we replaced this part of free solvent with 2-methyloxolane (MO) which has a lower melting point ( $-136^{\circ}C$ , Table S1) and is less polar. Through this strategy, not only the co-embeddable solvation structure is retained and the ion transport kinetics are accelerated, but also the working temperature range of electrolyte in low-temperature environment is significantly widened by increasing the solvation entropy. To highlight the progressiveness of our designed electrolyte, we also used common co-intercalation ether electrolyte (CCE) and WSE as controls, and the specific electrolyte formulation is shown in Table S2. According to the optical photographs in Figure S1, CCE starts to have salt precipitation at $-30^{\circ}C$ , and it is even completely solidified at $-50^{\circ}C$ . On the other hand, WSE and our CIE remain liquid at $-50^{\circ}C$ , which effectively guarantees the possibility of electrolyte application at low temperatures. The ion transport mechanisms of various electrolytes at low temperatures are shown in Fig. 1, among which the CIE has the fastest ion transport rate due to the presence of the co-intercalation behavior.

citations.quote: When the temperature is lower than -20 °C, the ionic conductivity of CCE decreases rapidly, which can be attributed to the precipitation of $NaPF_{6}$ in the electrolyte. While CIE maintains a high ionic conductivity at low temperatures and is always higher than that of WSE. Therefore, compared to the WSE, the CIE designed here can effectively solve the decrease in ionic conductivity and promote ion transport at low temperatures. In addition, we also tested the physical parameters of different electrolytes, such as the electrochemical window and transference number (Figs. S5, S6). Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were carried out to further investigate the solvation structure of the electrolyte under different temperature gradients. The radial distribution functions (RDF) of different electrolytes are shown in Fig. 2e,f and S7-8. In CCE, the average coordination number of G2 is 1.60 and that of PF $_{6}^{-}$ is 0.87. While in CIE, the coordination number of G2 decreases to 1.41, the coordination number of PF $_{6}^{-}$ increases to 1.10, and that of MO is 0.11. This is attributed to the introduction of MO which has a dipole interaction with G2, slightly weakening the coordination of G2 and Na $^{+}$ . In addition, MO hardly coordinates with Na $^{+}$ , which is consistent with the results of Raman and FTIR. In WSE, the average coordination number of MO is 0.93 and PF $_{6}^{-}$ is 3.05, constituting a typical aggregate-type (AGG) solvation structure rich in anions.

association_citations.quote: The MO solvent is added into linear ether G2 to precisely regulate the solvation structure and expand the electrolyte's low-temperature range via an entropy-driven effect. Experiments and simulations reveal that the $Na^{+}-G2$ chelating coordination structure can be well co-embedded in HC negative electrode, avoiding the sluggish traditional desolvation process and significantly improving ion diffusion at low temperatures. Meanwhile, the high sodium salt dissociation ability of G2 ensures good ionic conductivity in electrolyte. And the dipole interaction between solvents drives an appropriate number of anions into the solvation sheath, inducing the formation of a thin layer of inorganic-rich SEI. This multi-scale synergistic design enables highly reversible and high-rate sodium storage at low temperatures. Consequently, the CIE enables HC to deliver an initial Coulombic efficiency of 80.5% at $-50\ ^{\circ}C$ and a capacity retention of 93% after 200 cycles. Moreover, an Ah-level full cell retains 163 Wh kg $^{-1}$ at 25 ${}^{\circ}C$ and 107 Wh kg $^{-1}$ at $-50\ ^{\circ}C$ . This study demonstrates the significance of the solvent co-embedding mechanism in improving low-temperature ion storage and provides a strategy for designing electrolytes toward cold environments.

Sodium hexafluorophosphate (NaPF $_6$ ), ethylene carbonate (EC), and methyl ethyl carbonate (EMC) were supplied by Guangzhou Tinci Materials Technology Co., Ltd. A baseline electrolyte was prepared by dissolving NaPF $_6$ (1 mol/L) into a mixed solvent of EC and EMC (weight ratio 3:7). To formulate a functional electrolyte, 1 wt% 2-Sulfobenzoic anhydride (SA) was added to the baseline system. The NFM cathode and hard carbon (HC) anode active materials were procured from Jiangsu Xiangying New Energy Technology Co., Ltd. and Kuraray Co., Ltd., respectively. The NFM cathode slurry consisted of 94.5 wt% NFM, 1.8 wt% PVDF, 1 wt% carbon nanotubes (CNT), 2.5 wt% Super P, and 0.2 wt% maleic acid dispersed in $N$ -methylpyrrolidone (NMP), and was cast onto aluminum foil. The HC anode was composed of 95 wt% HC,

![](images/8bfcb630e9de984c98fbfc69f2dd0cb440e9bd8293373fa0ec9806e9fb6d55de.jpg)  
Fig. 1. 2-Sulfobenzoic anhydride (SA) is introduced as electrolyte additive to enhance the electrochemical performance of pouch SIBs.

1.5 wt% carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC), 2 wt% styrene-butadiene rubber (SBR), and 1.5 wt% Super P. A Celgard 2700 membrane (Xingyuan Materials Co., Ltd.) was employed as the separator. The areal mass loadings of the cathode and anode were 33.0 and 20.1 mg/cm $^{2}$ , respectively, with a negative-to-positive (N/P) capacity ratio of 1.1 (based on theoretical capacity calculation).

evidence_ledger.quote: Under more extreme conditions, discharge tests at $-20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ (Fig. 4a) revealed that cells with SA-based electrolyte delivered discharge capacities of 758.6, 702.2 and $638.2\mathrm{mAh}$ at $0.2\mathrm{C}$ , $0.5\mathrm{C}$ , and $1\mathrm{C}$ ( $1\mathrm{C} = 900\mathrm{mA}$ ), respectively, outperforming those with the baseline electrolyte, which exhibited 706.3, 636.8 and $563.6\mathrm{mAh}$ . These results confirm that SA facilitates higher energy density and improved capacity retention at low temperatures, rendering it well-suited for emergency storage applications in cold environments. In addition, the rate capability of sodium-ion batteries at ambient temperature is critical for practical deployment. High-rate performance enables rapid charge/discharge cycles, a requirement for power-intensive applications such as electric vehicles and portable electronics [27a,28]. As shown in Fig. 4d, the SA containing system exhibited superior rate capacity, indicating enhanced commercial viability. Long-term cycling at 1C was also evaluated at room temperature (Figs. 4c and S7). During extended cycling, the baseline electrolyte showed faster polarization growth, whereas the SA-based system demonstrated superior capacity retention and enhanced coulombic efficiency. These characteristics contribute to reduced energy losses and extended battery lifespan, which are advantageous for grid-scale and commercial energy storage [29].

evidence_ledger.quote: Pouch cells were subjected to aging and pre-formation process, both conducted under pressure by charging from open-circuit voltage (OCV) to 3.8 V at 45 °C. Long-term cycling was carried out on a five-channel battery testing system. Cells were charged at a constant current of 900 mA to a cutoff voltage of 3.8 V, followed by a constant voltage hold at 3.8 V until the current decreased to 30 mA, and subsequently discharged at 900 mA down to 1.5 V. Discharge was carried out at 900 mA down to 1.5 V. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was measured using an AMETEK Solartron Analytical system over a frequency range of 100 kHz to 0.04 Hz. Galvanostatic intermittent titration technique (GITT) measurements were conducted using a discharge current of 45 mA, with a discharge duration of 1 h followed by a rest period of 2 h. Tafel analysis was conducted using Na|Na symmetric coin cells on an electrochemical workstation over a voltage range of -0.13 to 0.13 V. The intersection of the linear portions of the two semi-logarithmic curves indicates the exchange current, from which the exchange current density was determined by normalizing the current to the surface area of the coin cell. Linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) was conducted on a CHI660E electrochemical workstation (Chenhua, Shanghai).

evidence_ledger.quote: When the little amount of the additive is used, the formed SEI film is not dense enough. On the contrary, the large amount of the additive forms a too thick SEI film, increasing the impedance. The discharge rate performance of the battery with G1 is the worst, owing to the decomposition of the electrolyte to form the SEI film with a high impedance [24]. From the discharge voltage curves at 2.0 C in Fig. 1C, the battery with G1 showed the lowest discharge voltage plateau, indicating a large impedance at large discharge rates, which is consistent with the rate results. The discharge capacities at high and low temperatures are shown in Fig. 3A. When setting the discharge capacity of each battery at 25 °C and 0.5C as the initial capacity (100%), the discharge capacities of the batteries with G1, G2, G3 and G4 at -20 °C and 0.2 C were 67.35%, 75.07%, 76.45%, and 74.26%, respectively. Hence, the capacity of the battery with G3 (3% ADN) was most significantly increased by up to 13% (Fig. 3B). At -10 °C and 0.5 C, the capacities were 72%, 78.17%, 80.21%, and 77.84%, respectively, from which the battery with G3 still exhibited the best performance with a discharge capacity improvement of nearly 8% (Fig. 3C). Similar results were presented at 45 °C and 1.0 C, where the capacities were 70.88%, 79.76%, 81.38%, 75.99%, respectively, and the batteries of G3 increased the discharge capacity by 10.5% (Fig. 3D). The specific discharge capacities at different temperatures are shown in Fig. 4.

evidence_ledger.quote: $Na_{0.76}Ni_{0.3}Fe_{0.4}Mn_{0.3}O_{2}$ , carbon nanotubes (CNTs), polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF), and carbon black with the mass ratio of 92.5: 2.0: 3.5: 2.0 were mixed in pyrrolidone to form a uniform slurry, and then coated on a 14 um thick aluminum foil to prepare the cathode electrode. The areal density was measured to be 10.0 mg cm $^{-2}$ , and the compacted density was 2.1 g cm $^{-3}$ . To prepare the anode electrode, hard carbon (Kuraray), carbon black, cellulose sodium (CMC), and styrene butadiene rubber (SBR) with the mass ratio of 94.5: 1.0: 2.0: 2.5 were added in deionized water and stirred into a uniform slurry, and then coated on a 9 um thick copper foil with the areal and compacted densities of 4.31 mg cm $^{-2}$ and 1.4 g cm $^{-3}$ , respectively. The cathode, anode, and separator (20 μm polypropylene) were assembled into pouch cells with a designed capacity of 650 mAh, and the thickness, width, and length were 10, 68, and 127 mm, respectively. The cells were dried in vacuum (-99 kPa/80 °C) until the water content was less than 150 ppm. At a dewpoint of -40 °C, the electrolytes defined as G1, G2, G3, and G4 (Table 1) were injected into the cells. After packaging in vacuum at room temperature for 48 hours; the pouch cells were placed at the environment with 0.8 MPa and 45 °C and charged at 0.05 C for 180 min, followed by another charge at a constant current of 0.1 C for 360 min.

Materials
The sodium hexafluorophosphate (NaPF $_6$ , 99.8% min), diethylene glycol dimethyl ether (G2, 99.8% min) and 2-methyloxolane (MO, 99.8% min) were purchased from DoDo Chem. Common ether electrolyte (CCE) was prepared by dissolving 0.8 M NaPF $_6$ in G2 solvent. Weakly solvated electrolyte (WSE) was prepared by dissolving 0.8 M NaPF $_6$ in MO solvent. Co-intercalated electrolyte (CIE) was prepared by dissolving 0.8 M NaPF $_6$ in G2: MO = 7:3 vol%. All electrolyte preparation processes were carried out in a glovebox filled with Ar (H $_2$ O < 0.1 ppm and O $_2$ < 0.1 ppm). The electrolyte salts and solvents we purchased are of anhydrous grade. After purchase, they are placed in the glove box for direct use.

Hard carbon (HC) materials were purchased from Baisige New Energy Co., Ltd. The HC negative electrode was prepared by mixing the active material, CMC (CMC2200, purchased from Daicel Corporation), SBR (BM-451B, purchased from Zeon Corporation) and conductive carbon black (weight ratio 92:1.5:3.5:3) in deionized water to form a homogeneous slurry. The slurry was spread on a copper foil (thickness 18 $\mu$ m) and dried at 80 °C for 8–12 h. Then, it was perforated into a circular electrode sheet with a diameter of 12 mm and a loading of 2.5–3.0 mg cm $^{-2}$ . Glass fiber (GF/D, Whatman) was used as separator and metallic sodium (purchased from Canrd Technology Co. Ltd.) was used as counter electrode. These components were assembled with HC negative electrode to assemble Na ||HC coin cells. The diameter of the glass fiber is 16 mm and the thickness is 0.68 mm. The diameter of the sodium metal electrode is 15.6 mm and the thickness is 0.4 mm.

The Ah-level pouch batteries were composed of O3-NaNi $_{1/3}$ Fe $_{1/3}$ Mn $_{1/3}$ O $_{2}$ (NFM) positive electrode and HC negative electrode coated on Al foil. The specific details and parameters are shown in Table S7.

As the temperature decreases, we verify the possibility of its operation at low temperatures, at -50 °C, the pouch cell still provides a capacity of 0.79 Ah (107 Wh kg $^{-1}$ ), demonstrating a significantly better low-temperature adaptability than that of conventional electrolytes. evidence_ledger.chunk_id: 0045_Lu 等 - 2025 - All-climate carbonate electrolyte with 2-sulfobenzoic anhydride additive leads the way to high-perfo::sec2::child0
evidence_ledger.paper_id: 0045_Lu 等 - 2025 - All-climate carbonate electrolyte with 2-sulfobenzoic anhydride additive leads the way to high-perfo
evidence_ledger.quote: A multifunctional additive, 2-sulfobenzoic anhydride (SA), was synthesized from the readily available saccharin, then 1 % SA was added into carbonate-based electrolytes to enhance the performance of pouch sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) employing $NaNi_{0.33}Fe_{0.33}Mn_{0.33}O_{2}$ (NFM) cathodes and hard carbon (HC) anodes across a wide temperature range from $-20\ ^{\circ}C$ to $60\ ^{\circ}C$ . The commercial pouch cells delivered a capacity retention of 90.52 % after 300 cycles at room temperature and 92.28 % after 300 cycles at $45\ ^{\circ}C$ . Low-temperature rate performance at $-20\ ^{\circ}C$ and cycling at $-10\ ^{\circ}C$ further demonstrated the excellent adaptability of SA-containing electrolytes under sub-zero temperature. Moreover, under high-voltage operation at 4.0 V, the SA-containing electrolyte effectively suppressed capacity fading, resulting in an 11.44 % improvement in capacity retention. Compared to conventional commercial electrolytes, this electrolyte enables interfacial optimization by suppressing excessive growth of cathode and anode interphases, also it eliminates detrimental electrolyte components, tune the solvation structure and promote interfacial reaction kinetics. In situ gas analysis conducted during cycling at $45\ ^{\circ}C$ revealed that SA significantly inhibits gas-evolving side reactions, thereby ensuring the safety of SIBs.

evidence_ledger.quote: In summary, a commercially feasible sodium-ion pouch cell with $Na_{0.76}Ni_{0.3}Fe_{0.4}Mn_{0.3}O_{2}$ /hard carbon is fabricated in this work. According to the calculation of the frontier molecular orbital energy, the electrolyte additive adiponitrile (ADN) is selected as the electrolyte additive to improve the performance of sodium-ion battery for the first time, and the effects of the ADN on the performance improvement of the cathode material $Na_{0.76}Ni_{0.3}Fe_{0.4}Mn_{0.3}O_{2}$ are investigated for the first time. The results show that ADN can promote the formation of highly conductive and stable SEI film on the cathode material surface, and effectively improve the high-low-temperature performance and cycling stability of $Na_{0.76}Ni_{0.3}Fe_{0.4}Mn_{0.3}O_{2}$ as the cathode electrode material of sodium-ion batteries. In particular, the battery with 3% ADN shows the most obvious improvement, its discharge capacity increases by 10.5%, 8%, and 13% at the operating temperature of 45, -10, and -20 °C, respectively. For the cycling stability, the capacity retention rate of the battery without adding ADN drops rapidly to 75% after 40 cycles, while the capacity retention rate of the battery with 3% ADN can still reach 78% after 220 cycles. Adding ADN as electrolyte additive effectively improves the electrochemical performance of sodium ion batteries.

evidence_ledger.quote: To solve this problem, a CIE was designed in this work. The design principle is based on the following findings: there are always some solvents in the electrolyte that do not participate in the coordination and only act as ion transport media, which are called free solvents. For this reason, we replaced this part of free solvent with 2-methyloxolane (MO) which has a lower melting point ( $-136^{\circ}C$ , Table S1) and is less polar. Through this strategy, not only the co-embeddable solvation structure is retained and the ion transport kinetics are accelerated, but also the working temperature range of electrolyte in low-temperature environment is significantly widened by increasing the solvation entropy. To highlight the progressiveness of our designed electrolyte, we also used common co-intercalation ether electrolyte (CCE) and WSE as controls, and the specific electrolyte formulation is shown in Table S2. According to the optical photographs in Figure S1, CCE starts to have salt precipitation at $-30^{\circ}C$ , and it is even completely solidified at $-50^{\circ}C$ . On the other hand, WSE and our CIE remain liquid at $-50^{\circ}C$ , which effectively guarantees the possibility of electrolyte application at low temperatures. The ion transport mechanisms of various electrolytes at low temperatures are shown in Fig. 1, among which the CIE has the fastest ion transport rate due to the presence of the co-intercalation behavior.

evidence_ledger.quote: When the temperature is lower than -20 °C, the ionic conductivity of CCE decreases rapidly, which can be attributed to the precipitation of $NaPF_{6}$ in the electrolyte. While CIE maintains a high ionic conductivity at low temperatures and is always higher than that of WSE. Therefore, compared to the WSE, the CIE designed here can effectively solve the decrease in ionic conductivity and promote ion transport at low temperatures. In addition, we also tested the physical parameters of different electrolytes, such as the electrochemical window and transference number (Figs. S5, S6). Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were carried out to further investigate the solvation structure of the electrolyte under different temperature gradients. The radial distribution functions (RDF) of different electrolytes are shown in Fig. 2e,f and S7-8. In CCE, the average coordination number of G2 is 1.60 and that of PF $_{6}^{-}$ is 0.87. While in CIE, the coordination number of G2 decreases to 1.41, the coordination number of PF $_{6}^{-}$ increases to 1.10, and that of MO is 0.11. This is attributed to the introduction of MO which has a dipole interaction with G2, slightly weakening the coordination of G2 and Na $^{+}$ . In addition, MO hardly coordinates with Na $^{+}$ , which is consistent with the results of Raman and FTIR. In WSE, the average coordination number of MO is 0.93 and PF $_{6}^{-}$ is 3.05, constituting a typical aggregate-type (AGG) solvation structure rich in anions.

evidence_ledger.quote: The MO solvent is added into linear ether G2 to precisely regulate the solvation structure and expand the electrolyte's low-temperature range via an entropy-driven effect. Experiments and simulations reveal that the $Na^{+}-G2$ chelating coordination structure can be well co-embedded in HC negative electrode, avoiding the sluggish traditional desolvation process and significantly improving ion diffusion at low temperatures. Meanwhile, the high sodium salt dissociation ability of G2 ensures good ionic conductivity in electrolyte. And the dipole interaction between solvents drives an appropriate number of anions into the solvation sheath, inducing the formation of a thin layer of inorganic-rich SEI. This multi-scale synergistic design enables highly reversible and high-rate sodium storage at low temperatures. Consequently, the CIE enables HC to deliver an initial Coulombic efficiency of 80.5% at $-50\ ^{\circ}C$ and a capacity retention of 93% after 200 cycles. citations.quote: A multifunctional additive, 2-sulfobenzoic anhydride (SA), was synthesized from the readily available saccharin, then 1 % SA was added into carbonate-based electrolytes to enhance the performance of pouch sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) employing $NaNi_{0.33}Fe_{0.33}Mn_{0.33}O_{2}$ (NFM) cathodes and hard carbon (HC) anodes across a wide temperature range from $-20\ ^{\circ}C$ to $60\ ^{\circ}C$ . The commercial pouch cells delivered a capacity retention of 90.52 % after 300 cycles at room temperature and 92.28 % after 300 cycles at $45\ ^{\circ}C$ . Low-temperature rate performance at $-20\ ^{\circ}C$ and cycling at $-10\ ^{\circ}C$ further demonstrated the excellent adaptability of SA-containing electrolytes under sub-zero temperature. Moreover, under high-voltage operation at 4.0 V, the SA-containing electrolyte effectively suppressed capacity fading, resulting in an 11.44 % improvement in capacity retention. Compared to conventional commercial electrolytes, this electrolyte enables interfacial optimization by suppressing excessive growth of cathode and anode interphases, also it eliminates detrimental electrolyte components, tune the solvation structure and promote interfacial reaction kinetics. In situ gas analysis conducted during cycling at $45\ ^{\circ}C$ revealed that SA significantly inhibits gas-evolving side reactions, thereby ensuring the safety of SIBs.

citations.quote: Under more extreme conditions, discharge tests at $-20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ (Fig. 4a) revealed that cells with SA-based electrolyte delivered discharge capacities of 758.6, 702.2 and $638.2\mathrm{mAh}$ at $0.2\mathrm{C}$ , $0.5\mathrm{C}$ , and $1\mathrm{C}$ ( $1\mathrm{C} = 900\mathrm{mA}$ ), respectively, outperforming those with the baseline electrolyte, which exhibited 706.3, 636.8 and $563.6\mathrm{mAh}$ . These results confirm that SA facilitates higher energy density and improved capacity retention at low temperatures, rendering it well-suited for emergency storage applications in cold environments. In addition, the rate capability of sodium-ion batteries at ambient temperature is critical for practical deployment. High-rate performance enables rapid charge/discharge cycles, a requirement for power-intensive applications such as electric vehicles and portable electronics [27a,28]. As shown in Fig. 4d, the SA containing system exhibited superior rate capacity, indicating enhanced commercial viability. Long-term cycling at 1C was also evaluated at room temperature (Figs. 4c and S7). During extended cycling, the baseline electrolyte showed faster polarization growth, whereas the SA-based system demonstrated superior capacity retention and enhanced coulombic efficiency. These characteristics contribute to reduced energy losses and extended battery lifespan, which are advantageous for grid-scale and commercial energy storage [29].

citations.chunk_id: 0045_Lu 等 - 2025 - All-climate carbonate electrolyte with 2-sulfobenzoic anhydride additive leads the way to high-perfo::sec2::child0
citations.quote: A multifunctional additive, 2-sulfobenzoic anhydride (SA), was synthesized from the readily available saccharin, then 1 % SA was added into carbonate-based electrolytes to enhance the performance of pouch sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) employing $NaNi_{0.33}Fe_{0.33}Mn_{0.33}O_{2}$ (NFM) cathodes and hard carbon (HC) anodes across a wide temperature range from $-20\ ^{\circ}C$ to $60\ ^{\circ}C$ . The commercial pouch cells delivered a capacity retention of 90.52 % after 300 cycles at room temperature and 92.28 % after 300 cycles at $45\ ^{\circ}C$ . Low-temperature rate performance at $-20\ ^{\circ}C$ and cycling at $-10\ ^{\circ}C$ further demonstrated the excellent adaptability of SA-containing electrolytes under sub-zero temperature. Moreover, under high-voltage operation at 4.0 V, the SA-containing electrolyte effectively suppressed capacity fading, resulting in an 11.44 % improvement in capacity retention. Compared to conventional commercial electrolytes, this electrolyte enables interfacial optimization by suppressing excessive growth of cathode and anode interphases, also it eliminates detrimental electrolyte components, tune the solvation structure and promote interfacial reaction kinetics. In situ gas analysis conducted during cycling at $45\ ^{\circ}C$ revealed that SA significantly inhibits gas-evolving side reactions, thereby ensuring the safety of SIBs.

Xiaona Song $^{a,b}$ , Tao Meng $^{a}$ , Yaoming Deng $^{a,b}$ , Aimei Gao $^{a}$ , Junmin Nan $^{a}$ , Dong

Shu $^{a,c,d,*}$ , Fenyun Yi $^{a}$

$^{a}$ School of Chemistry and Environment, South China Normal University, Guangzhou 510006, PR China

$^{b}$ R&D centre, Dongguan McNair New Power Co., Ltd, Dongguan, Guangdong 523000, PR China

$^{d}$ Guangzhou Key Laboratory of Materials for Energy Conversion and Storage, Guangzhou 510006, PR China

\* Corresponding author E-mail address: dshu@scnu.edu.cn (Dong Shu)

Abstract: A commercially feasible sodium-ion pouch cell with a capacity of 650 mAh is fabricated using the ternary layered $\mathrm{Na_{0.76}Ni_{0.3}Fe_{0.4}Mn_{0.3}O_2}$ and the hard carbon as the cathode and anode materials, respectively. $1.0\mathrm{MNaPF}_6$ in the mixed carbonate solvents is served as the electrolyte. According to the calculation of the frontier molecular orbital energy, adiponitrile (ADN) has a stronger ability of electron donating than the carbonate solvents and thus is easier to be reduced on the surface of the cathode material to form the solid-electrolyte interphase (SEI) film, so ADN is selected as the electrolyte additive to improve the performance of sodium-ion battery for the first time.

2.2 Battery Assembly
$Na_{0.76}Ni_{0.3}Fe_{0.4}Mn_{0.3}O_{2}$ , carbon nanotubes (CNTs), polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF), and carbon black with the mass ratio of 92.5: 2.0: 3.5: 2.0 were mixed in pyrrolidone to form a uniform slurry, and then coated on a 14 um thick aluminum foil to prepare the cathode electrode. The areal density was measured to be 10.0 mg cm $^{-2}$ , and the compacted density was 2.1 g cm $^{-3}$ . To prepare the anode electrode, hard carbon (Kuraray), carbon black, cellulose sodium (CMC), and styrene butadiene rubber (SBR) with the mass ratio of 94.5: 1.0: 2.0: 2.5 were added in deionized water and stirred into a uniform slurry, and then coated on a 9 um thick copper foil with the areal and compacted densities of 4.31 mg cm $^{-2}$ and 1.4 g cm $^{-3}$ , respectively. The cathode, anode, and separator (20 μm polypropylene) were assembled into pouch cells with a designed capacity of 650 mAh, and the thickness, width, and length were 10, 68, and 127 mm, respectively. The cells were dried in vacuum (-99 kPa/80 °C) until the water content was less than 150 ppm. At a dewpoint of -40 °C, the electrolytes defined as G1, G2, G3, and G4 (Table 1) were injected into the cells. After packaging in vacuum at room temperature for 48 hours; the pouch cells were placed at the environment with 0.8 MPa and 45 °C and charged at 0.05 C for 180 min, followed by another charge at a constant current of 0.1 C for 360 min. Then, the pouch cells were punctuated in vacuum to remove excess electrolyte and gas generated by the side reactions during the charge process. citations.quote: In summary, a commercially feasible sodium-ion pouch cell with $Na_{0.76}Ni_{0.3}Fe_{0.4}Mn_{0.3}O_{2}$ /hard carbon is fabricated in this work. According to the calculation of the frontier molecular orbital energy, the electrolyte additive adiponitrile (ADN) is selected as the electrolyte additive to improve the performance of sodium-ion battery for the first time, and the effects of the ADN on the performance improvement of the cathode material $Na_{0.76}Ni_{0.3}Fe_{0.4}Mn_{0.3}O_{2}$ are investigated for the first time. The results show that ADN can promote the formation of highly conductive and stable SEI film on the cathode material surface, and effectively improve the high-low-temperature performance and cycling stability of $Na_{0.76}Ni_{0.3}Fe_{0.4}Mn_{0.3}O_{2}$ as the cathode electrode material of sodium-ion batteries. In particular, the battery with 3% ADN shows the most obvious improvement, its discharge capacity increases by 10.5%, 8%, and 13% at the operating temperature of 45, -10, and -20 °C, respectively. For the cycling stability, the capacity retention rate of the battery without adding ADN drops rapidly to 75% after 40 cycles, while the capacity retention rate of the battery with 3% ADN can still reach 78% after 220 cycles. Adding ADN as electrolyte additive effectively improves the electrochemical performance of sodium ion batteries.

citations.quote: When the little amount of the additive is used, the formed SEI film is not dense enough. On the contrary, the large amount of the additive forms a too thick SEI film, increasing the impedance. The discharge rate performance of the battery with G1 is the worst, owing to the decomposition of the electrolyte to form the SEI film with a high impedance [24]. From the discharge voltage curves at 2.0 C in Fig. 1C, the battery with G1 showed the lowest discharge voltage plateau, indicating a large impedance at large discharge rates, which is consistent with the rate results. The discharge capacities at high and low temperatures are shown in Fig. 3A. When setting the discharge capacity of each battery at 25 °C and 0.5C as the initial capacity (100%), the discharge capacities of the batteries with G1, G2, G3 and G4 at -20 °C and 0.2 C were 67.35%, 75.07%, 76.45%, and 74.26%, respectively. Hence, the capacity of the battery with G3 (3% ADN) was most significantly increased by up to 13% (Fig. 3B). At -10 °C and 0.5 C, the capacities were 72%, 78.17%, 80.21%, and 77.84%, respectively, from which the battery with G3 still exhibited the best performance with a discharge capacity improvement of nearly 8% (Fig. 3C). Similar results were presented at 45 °C and 1.0 C, where the capacities were 70.88%, 79.76%, 81.38%, 75.99%, respectively, and the batteries of G3 increased the discharge capacity by 10.5% (Fig. 3D). The specific discharge capacities at different temperatures are shown in Fig. 4.

Abstract: A commercially feasible sodium-ion pouch cell with a capacity of 650 mAh is fabricated using the ternary layered $\mathrm{Na_{0.76}Ni_{0.3}Fe_{0.4}Mn_{0.3}O_2}$ and the hard carbon as the cathode and anode materials, respectively. $1.0\mathrm{MNaPF}_6$ in the mixed carbonate solvents is served as the electrolyte. According to the calculation of the frontier molecular orbital energy, adiponitrile (ADN) has a stronger ability of electron donating than the carbonate solvents and thus is easier to be reduced on the surface of the cathode material to form the solid-electrolyte interphase (SEI) film, so ADN is selected as the electrolyte additive to improve the performance of sodium-ion battery for the first time.

citations.quote:
2.2 Battery Assembly
$Na_{0.76}Ni_{0.3}Fe_{0.4}Mn_{0.3}O_{2}$ , carbon nanotubes (CNTs), polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF), and carbon black with the mass ratio of 92.5: 2.0: 3.5: 2.0 were mixed in pyrrolidone to form a uniform slurry, and then coated on a 14 um thick aluminum foil to prepare the cathode electrode. The areal density was measured to be 10.0 mg cm $^{-2}$ , and the compacted density was 2.1 g cm $^{-3}$ . To prepare the anode electrode, hard carbon (Kuraray), carbon black, cellulose sodium (CMC), and styrene butadiene rubber (SBR) with the mass ratio of 94.5: 1.0: 2.0: 2.5 were added in deionized water and stirred into a uniform slurry, and then coated on a 9 um thick copper foil with the areal and compacted densities of 4.31 mg cm $^{-2}$ and 1.4 g cm $^{-3}$ , respectively. The cathode, anode, and separator (20 μm polypropylene) were assembled into pouch cells with a designed capacity of 650 mAh, and the thickness, width, and length were 10, 68, and 127 mm, respectively. The cells were dried in vacuum (-99 kPa/80 °C) until the water content was less than 150 ppm. At a dewpoint of -40 °C, the electrolytes defined as G1, G2, G3, and G4 (Table 1) were injected into the cells. After packaging in vacuum at room temperature for 48 hours; the pouch cells were placed at the environment with 0.8 MPa and 45 °C and charged at 0.05 C for 180 min, followed by another charge at a constant current of 0.1 C for 360 min. Then, the pouch cells were punctuated in vacuum to remove excess electrolyte and gas generated by the side reactions during the charge process. Eventually, the cells were packaged again and cut the air-bags to obtain the finished batteries for testing.

On the contrary, the large amount of the additive forms a too thick SEI film, increasing the impedance. The discharge rate performance of the battery with G1 is the worst, owing to the decomposition of the electrolyte to form the SEI film with a high impedance [24]. From the discharge voltage curves at 2.0 C in Fig. 1C, the battery with G1 showed the lowest discharge voltage plateau, indicating a large impedance at large discharge rates, which is consistent with the rate results. The discharge capacities at high and low temperatures are shown in Fig. 3A. When setting the discharge capacity of each battery at 25 °C and 0.5C as the initial capacity (100%), the discharge capacities of the batteries with G1, G2, G3 and G4 at -20 °C and 0.2 C were 67.35%, 75.07%, 76.45%, and 74.26%, respectively. At -10 °C and 0.5 C, the capacities were 72%, 78.17%, 80.21%, and 77.84%, respectively, from which the battery with G3 still exhibited the best performance with a discharge capacity improvement of nearly 8% (Fig. 3C). Similar results were presented at 45 °C and 1.0 C, where the capacities were 70.88%, 79.76%, 81.38%, 75.99%, respectively, and the batteries of G3 increased the discharge capacity by 10.5% (Fig. 3D). The specific discharge capacities at different temperatures are shown in Fig. 4.

citations.chunk_id: 0033_Li 等 - 2026 - Enhanced sodium storage in hard carbon via solvent co-intercalation electrolyte enabling Ah-level po::sec7
citations.quote:
Materials
The sodium hexafluorophosphate (NaPF $_6$ , 99.8% min), diethylene glycol dimethyl ether (G2, 99.8% min) and 2-methyloxolane (MO, 99.8% min) were purchased from DoDo Chem. Common ether electrolyte (CCE) was prepared by dissolving 0.8 M NaPF $_6$ in G2 solvent. Weakly solvated electrolyte (WSE) was prepared by dissolving 0.8 M NaPF $_6$ in MO solvent. Co-intercalated electrolyte (CIE) was prepared by dissolving 0.8 M NaPF $_6$ in G2: MO = 7:3 vol%. All electrolyte preparation processes were carried out in a glovebox filled with Ar (H $_2$ O < 0.1 ppm and O $_2$ < 0.1 ppm). The electrolyte salts and solvents we purchased are of anhydrous grade. After purchase, they are placed in the glove box for direct use.

Hard carbon (HC) materials were purchased from Baisige New Energy Co., Ltd. The HC negative electrode was prepared by mixing the active material, CMC (CMC2200, purchased from Daicel Corporation), SBR (BM-451B, purchased from Zeon Corporation) and conductive carbon black (weight ratio 92:1.5:3.5:3) in deionized water to form a homogeneous slurry. The slurry was spread on a copper foil (thickness 18 $\mu$ m) and dried at 80 °C for 8–12 h. Then, it was perforated into a circular electrode sheet with a diameter of 12 mm and a loading of 2.5–3.0 mg cm $^{-2}$ . Glass fiber (GF/D, Whatman) was used as separator and metallic sodium (purchased from Canrd Technology Co. Ltd.) was used as counter electrode. These components were assembled with HC negative electrode to assemble Na ||HC coin cells. The diameter of the glass fiber is 16 mm and the thickness is 0.68 mm. The diameter of the sodium metal electrode is 15.6 mm and the thickness is 0.4 mm.

The Ah-level pouch batteries were composed of O3-NaNi $_{1/3}$ Fe $_{1/3}$ Mn $_{1/3}$ O $_{2}$ (NFM) positive electrode and HC negative electrode coated on Al foil. The specific details and parameters are shown in Table S7.

citations.quote: To verify the practical applicability of CIE, we assembled a 1.2 Ah (163 Wh kg $^{-1}$ ) pouch cell with O3-type NFM positive electrode and HC negative electrode (Fig. 6a). Figure 6b shows the cycling performance of the pouch cell at different temperatures. At 25 °C, the pouch cell provides a capacity of 1.18 Ah. As the temperature decreases, we verify the possibility of its operation at low temperatures, at -50 °C, the pouch cell still provides a capacity of 0.79 Ah (107 Wh kg $^{-1}$ ), demonstrating a significantly better low-temperature adaptability than that of conventional electrolytes. Moreover, even at -50 °C, the charge/discharge curve maintains a stable voltage plateau (Fig. 6c). Figure 6d shows the cycling performance of the pouch cell at -20 °C with 94.1% capacity retention after 300 cycles. In addition, in order to visually verify the practical application potential, the LED lights are continuously powered at a low temperature of -50 °C. The fully-charged state pouch cells keep the LED lights working for more than 10 hours (Fig. 6e). This demonstration confirms that the CIE has good prospects for practical applications, especially at low temperatures. We further compare our results with some previously reported low-temperature sodium-ion pouch cells (Fig. 6f, Table S6) $^{26,52-58}$ , and our work is comparable to most of the advanced reported works, which fully proves that the CIE developed by us has important application value for SIBs in cold environments.

citations.quote: To solve this problem, a CIE was designed in this work. The design principle is based on the following findings: there are always some solvents in the electrolyte that do not participate in the coordination and only act as ion transport media, which are called free solvents. For this reason, we replaced this part of free solvent with 2-methyloxolane (MO) which has a lower melting point ( $-136^{\circ}C$ , Table S1) and is less polar. Through this strategy, not only the co-embeddable solvation structure is retained and the ion transport kinetics are accelerated, but also the working temperature range of electrolyte in low-temperature environment is significantly widened by increasing the solvation entropy. To highlight the progressiveness of our designed electrolyte, we also used common co-intercalation ether electrolyte (CCE) and WSE as controls, and the specific electrolyte formulation is shown in Table S2. According to the optical photographs in Figure S1, CCE starts to have salt precipitation at $-30^{\circ}C$ , and it is even completely solidified at $-50^{\circ}C$ . On the other hand, WSE and our CIE remain liquid at $-50^{\circ}C$ , which effectively guarantees the possibility of electrolyte application at low temperatures. The ion transport mechanisms of various electrolytes at low temperatures are shown in Fig. 1, among which the CIE has the fastest ion transport rate due to the presence of the co-intercalation behavior.

citations.chunk_id: 0033_Li 等 - 2026 - Enhanced sodium storage in hard carbon via solvent co-intercalation electrolyte enabling Ah-level po::sec2::child6
citations.quote: When the temperature is lower than -20 °C, the ionic conductivity of CCE decreases rapidly, which can be attributed to the precipitation of $NaPF_{6}$ in the electrolyte. While CIE maintains a high ionic conductivity at low temperatures and is always higher than that of WSE. Therefore, compared to the WSE, the CIE designed here can effectively solve the decrease in ionic conductivity and promote ion transport at low temperatures. In addition, we also tested the physical parameters of different electrolytes, such as the electrochemical window and transference number (Figs. S5, S6). Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were carried out to further investigate the solvation structure of the electrolyte under different temperature gradients. The radial distribution functions (RDF) of different electrolytes are shown in Fig. 2e,f and S7-8. In CCE, the average coordination number of G2 is 1.60 and that of PF $_{6}^{-}$ is 0.87. While in CIE, the coordination number of G2 decreases to 1.41, the coordination number of PF $_{6}^{-}$ increases to 1.10, and that of MO is 0.11. This is attributed to the introduction of MO which has a dipole interaction with G2, slightly weakening the coordination of G2 and Na $^{+}$ . In addition, MO hardly coordinates with Na $^{+}$ , which is consistent with the results of Raman and FTIR. In WSE, the average coordination number of MO is 0.93 and PF $_{6}^{-}$ is 3.05, constituting a typical aggregate-type (AGG) solvation structure rich in anions.
